Compare two research ideas for the SAME research problem and pick the stronger one.

Research problem: Can MVFA's segmentation adapters learn transferable localisation from image-level labels alone? Today they learn only from pixel masks of BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC. We replace the Dice and Focal seg_loss with a multiple-instance objective applied at all four levels to the segmentation-branch patch-to-text similarity map (mean of the top 2% patch anomaly probabilities; max and mean pooling as ablations), and train on all five source datasets with masks discarded. Primary question and hypothesis: because every patch is scored against a shared text anchor, image-level supervision aligns patch-level evidence with the text 'abnormal' direction, so the learned localisation transfers to the unseen modality and retains at least 80% of mask-supervised MVFA's pixel-level AUROC (with PRO and image AUROC also reported). A visual-only MIL control (same operator on a linear patch classifier without text anchors) tests whether text anchoring is responsible. Secondary analyses: per-level localisation quality, and a label-budget comparison on two held-out modalities between image-labelled training and mask-supervised training on 10%, 30% and 100% of the masked images.

A stronger idea is one whose proposed change acts on the SPECIFIC mechanism of the target method that causes the problem (here: the released MVFA code and its verified behaviour), rather than a generic improvement that would apply to any anomaly detector.

Judge on:
1. Specificity. Would this idea plausibly solve THIS problem in THIS method better than a generic alternative? A mechanism that applies equally to any model and any problem is WEAKER, not stronger, because it does not explain why it fixes this problem.
2. Evidence. Is the proposed mechanism supported by the cited literature or by verified properties of the code and the benchmark?
3. Testability. Does the idea make a concrete, falsifiable prediction that can be checked on BMAD with one Colab GPU?

Explicitly DO NOT reward: length or polish of the write-up, stacking many modules, vague "add an attention/adapter module" proposals, or ideas that need data, labels or compute that are not available.

Idea A:
TITLE: Graph-Laplacian smoothness regularisation for MIL-trained segmentation adapters
SUMMARY: Add to the image-level MIL loss a feature-weighted graph-Laplacian smoothness term on each level's patch anomaly map, so localisation learned from image labels forms coherent regions.
HYPOTHESIS: Feature-weighted Laplacian regularisation increases held-out PRO of MIL-trained segmentation adapters by at least 3 points and halves the number of spurious connected components per abnormal image, without reducing image AUROC by more than 1 point.
RESEARCH IDEA: Independent variable: regulariser (none vs. uniform 4-neighbour Laplacian vs. feature-weighted Laplacian). For level l, patch anomaly probabilities p (289), graph weights w_ij = exp(-||f_i - f_j||^2 / (2 sigma^2)) for 8-neighbours using frozen CLIP features, loss_smooth = sum_ij w_ij (p_i - p_j)^2 / sum_ij w_ij, added with weight lambda = 0.5 to top-k MIL (abnormal) and all-patches-normal (normal) losses. Dependent variables: pixel AUROC, PRO, a region-coherence measure (number of connected components above threshold per image), and image AUROC on held-out modalities.
RATIONALE: Image-level MIL supervises a handful of patches and leaves the rest of an abnormal image unconstrained, producing speckled maps (UltraAD reports that MVFA's maps already struggle to form continuous regions). A graph prior over the 17x17 patch grid that penalises disagreement between neighbouring, similar-looking patches would spread MIL evidence across coherent regions without masks.
METHOD: 1) loss.py: graph_smooth(p, feats) with precomputed 8-neighbour index pairs for the 17x17 grid; weights from L2-normalised frozen CLIP patch tokens of the same level (no gradient), sigma = median pairwise distance. 2) train_zero.py: seg loss = topk_mil + normal_all + lambda * graph_smooth at each level. 3) Hyper-parameters: k = 6, lambda in {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}, lr 1e-4, 50 epochs. 4) Inference unchanged.
EXPERIMENT: Protocol: BMAD zero-shot, leave-one-modality-out (RESC and OCT17 held out together); masks of the source datasets are discarded for all image-label-supervised variants; checkpoints selected on a validation split of the source modalities using image AUROC only (no masks used for selection); mask-supervised MVFA re-run under the same rule as the reference; 3 seeds; evaluation on the held-out modalities that have masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC) for pixel metrics and on all six for image AUROC. Baselines: mask-supervised MVFA; MIL only; MIL + uniform Laplacian. Ablations: lambda; neighbourhood (4 vs. 8); weights from CLIP vs. adapted features. Metrics: pixel AUROC, PRO, connected components per image, image AUROC. Falsification: no PRO gain over MIL only.

Idea B:
TITLE: Attribution-based pseudo-masks: gradient attribution of the detection branch's image score supervises the segmentation adapters
SUMMARY: Keep the detection-to-segmentation teacher idea but replace the detection branch's mean-pooled patch maps with Grad-CAM-style attributions of its image-level score to the patch tokens, filtered across levels, as pseudo-masks.
HYPOTHESIS: Attribution-derived pseudo-masks have at least 1.5x the pixel precision of raw detection-map pseudo-masks on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC training images, and segmentation adapters trained on them retain at least 75% of mask-supervised MVFA's held-out pixel-AUROC margin over chance.
RATIONALE: The reviewed weakness of the parent is that MVFA's detection branch is trained with a MEAN-pooled image loss (train_zero.py:130), so its raw patch map spreads evidence over many patches. What the image decision actually depends on is better measured by attribution: the gradient of the image score with respect to each patch token, weighted by the token, highlights patches that drive the decision. Substituting attribution for raw maps keeps the parent's framing (an image-label-trained teacher inside MVFA supervises the segmentation branch) and its evaluation.
METHOD: 1) Train detection adapters with their image-level BCE (unchanged). 2) For each abnormal source image, compute the image score s = sum_l mean_j p_lj (as in train_zero.py), backpropagate to the adapted patch tokens of each level, attribution a_lj = ReLU(<grad_lj, token_lj>), normalise per level; pseudo-mask patches = top 5% of attribution at >= 3 of 4 levels, foreground-restricted, upsampled to 240x240. 3) Train segmentation adapters with Focal + Dice on pseudo-masks (normal images: empty). 4) One refinement round. 5) Code: make_attr_masks.py (torch autograd on the frozen detection model), train_zero.py loss swap.
EXPERIMENT: BMAD zero-shot leave-one-modality-out (RESC and OCT17 held out together); no source masks used by the proposed variants; checkpoints selected on source-modality validation splits by image AUROC; mask-supervised MVFA re-run under the same rule as reference; 3 seeds; pixel metrics on held-out BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC. Baselines: mask-supervised MVFA; raw detection-map pseudo-masks (parent); asymmetric SigLIP-MIL. Ablations: attribution type (gradient x input vs. integrated gradients with 16 steps); top-percentage; agreement threshold. Metrics: pseudo-mask precision/IoU (analysis), held-out pixel AUROC, PRO, image AUROC. Falsification: precision not improved over raw maps.
